raw: For a first reading, follow Part I Sections 1--7. These sections establish the coordinate maps, filter transfers, exact reconstruction, and the separation of packet error from smooth approximation error. Section 11 develops finite adaptive selection. Sections 13--14 give the cyclic Smith realization. Continue with Part II Sections E2--E6 for lattice and stability generalizations, E7--E11 for singular packets and recovery, and E12--E14 for nonlinear and Cayley coordinates. Each visual plate identifies the corresponding manuscript result.

This chapter develops the signal realization of the projector-resolved seed calculus. The impulse $\delta_0$ is taken as a primitive signal seed and its shift orbit supplies the address system. Residue projectors split a sequence into exact polyphase channels, nested divisibility gives exact refinement, and every finite impulse-response operator becomes a matrix of packet transfers. The standard perfect-reconstruction condition for a filter bank is therefore an analysis--synthesis identity in the common operator language of the series. Haar analysis and every finite-depth wavelet-packet transform are treated on complex $\ell^2$, together with concrete finite-signal models and a predict--update lifting step. The edge problem is separated into two statements. When a discontinuity packet is known and retained exactly, approximation error is exactly the approximation error of the remaining smooth packet. No spectral approximation of the jump is performed. When the packet is estimated, a symmetric-difference bound isolates mask error, amplitude error, and smooth-background error. Numerical studies compare global Fourier truncation, exact known-packet reconstruction, and a deliberately narrow positive-contrast estimator in one and two dimensions, including curved boundaries, corners, and multiple amplitudes. The same cyclic phase action is then placed on the Smith reflection disk. Its pullback through the Cayley transform is a M\"obius action on impedance, and the two-phase case is precisely impedance--admittance inversion. Nonlinear coefficient products obey cyclic packet convolution. The accompanying formal development gives a Lean formalization of all twenty theorem-like statements under the hypotheses stated below: 225 supporting theorem targets in 23 modules. Eighteen regenerated figures, machine-readable numerical results, the 33-test original companion suite, and 36 additional exact-model and verifier tests accompany the chapter. Exact signal theorems, limited numerical estimators, classical constructions, and open recovery problems are kept distinct throughout.

The chapter proves exact polyphase reconstruction, exact finite filter-transfer identities, perfect reconstruction for the stated filter banks, the conditional known-edge theorem, mask and amplitude perturbation bounds, nonlinear residue-convolution laws, and the Smith-coordinate phase action. It does not claim that every discontinuity can be detected automatically, that every form of Gibbs ringing has been eliminated, or that the supplied two-class estimator is a universal segmentation method. The estimator is included as one reproducible finite example.  For every finite packet refinement tree, the chapter proves existence of a globally optimal complete pruning, an exact dynamic-programming selector for additive costs, and a deterministic margin-stability certificate. Wavelets, filter banks, the Cayley transform, and the classical Smith grid are treated as classical inputs organized in the common seed--packet--refinement language.

This chapter develops the transfer-semigroup realization of the projector-resolved seed calculus. A seed is propagated by a one-parameter semigroup, a Markov kernel, a normalized Bayesian transfer, a fractional spectral power, a Green operator, or a potential-weighted Feynman--Kac operator. Exact packet projectors resolve every transfer into input-output blocks, and the semigroup law becomes block convolution over intermediate packets. Coarse and fine generators are compared by a refinement defect. A Duhamel identity proves that this generator-level defect is exactly the source of the corresponding semigroup defect and gives a quantitative stability bound. In the stochastic realization, point-mass seeds generate random walks and continuous-time Markov evolution; exact lumpability is the vanishing of the same refinement defect. Conditional expectation is treated as a weighted orthogonal packet projector, with nested partitions producing martingale-difference packets. Bayesian conditioning is a normalized nonlinear operator. Its independent-data composition law, packet-evidence decomposition, stability bound, conjugate updates, and continuous likelihood flow are proved explicitly.  The Bayesian refinement conjecture is resolved in finite dimensions: for strictly positive likelihoods and at least two coarse packets, exact commutation for every prior is equivalent to blockwise-constant likelihoods up to global scale, and every failure factors through an explicit information-loss packet. Fractional powers are constructed packetwise through the spectral projectors of a positive operator, and the square-root semigroup is recovered by subordination. The fractional-naturality conjecture is also resolved for bounded nonnegative self-adjoint refinement systems: the fractional intertwining defect has an exact resolvent integral, a gap-free Hölder certificate, a sharper common-gap estimate, and a Duhamel semigroup bound. Green kernels, finite-difference Poisson problems, and second-order low-mode convergence provide the PDE realization. A finite-state Feynman--Kac formula is proved by path enumeration. Exact Schur--Feshbach elimination shows that discarded latent packets return as a frequency-dependent self-energy and, in time coordinates, as a memory kernel. Survival and hazard functions are generated by transient semigroups. Nineteen code-generated figures, machine-readable results, the original thirty-seven automated tests, and seventeen added boundary-case checks accompany this reviewed edition. The inherited September 6 release records five checked Lean blocks covering all 33 scoped theorem-like results in Appendix~\ref{core:sec:lean-status}. Finite-dimensional theorems, classical infinite-dimensional extensions, numerical certificates, and open continuum claims are kept separate.

\textbf{Scope and claim boundary.} The chapter proves the stated finite-dimensional semigroup, packet, Markov, Bayesian, conditional-expectation, fractional spectral, Green-kernel, Feynman--Kac, Schur--Feshbach, and survival identities. It also proves quantitative refinement-defect formulas under explicit norm hypotheses, including exact transfer of a bounded generator defect to every fractional power $0<\alpha<1$ for bounded nonnegative self-adjoint generators. It does not claim that an arbitrary infinite-dimensional operator generates a semigroup, that every stochastic process admits a finite packet representation, that every posterior family is conjugate, that finite Bayesian sufficiency automatically extends to infinite disintegrations, or that every PDE continuum limit follows from a finite test. Domain, closability, sectoriality, measurability, tightness, and compactness hypotheses remain necessary in their respective infinite-dimensional settings. Classical sources are retained in the separate end-of-series reference ledger rather than reproduced in this chapter.

The tests cover projector reconstruction, packet-block semigroup composition, exact and approximate Markov lumping, Bayesian composition and flow, the exact Bayesian refinement criterion, information-loss factorization, likelihood-profile partitions, conditional-expectation towers, Hermite orthogonality, fractional semigroups, square-root subordination, fractional intertwining and semigroup-defect bounds, discrete Green kernels, PDE convergence, Feynman--Kac enumeration, Schur--Feshbach elimination, memory kernels, refinement defects, hidden Markov filtering, and survival curves.

The transfer-semigroup realization gives one common operator language to several subjects that are often presented separately. Markov propagation is linear transfer of a probability seed. Conditional expectation is stochastic projection. Bayesian conditioning is normalized nonlinear transfer, and its exact finite coarsening law is characterized by packetwise likelihood sufficiency. Fractional calculus is spectral packet reweighting, and bounded positive refinement defects transfer to fractional powers and fractional semigroups by explicit resolvent and Duhamel estimates. A Green operator reconstructs a field from source packets. Feynman--Kac propagation adds path weights to stochastic transfer. Schur--Feshbach elimination shows that hidden packets are not destroyed; they return through self-energy and memory. Survival and hazard are scalar reconstructions of a transient semigroup.

A bounded generator and a finite packet system turn a semigroup into a matrix of transfer blocks. We prove convolution, differential, path, Laplace, resolvent, and defect formulas. Exact intertwining yields an inverse limit semigroup. Weighted summable adjacent defects give convergent reconstructed evolutions, while range leakage determines whether the limit remains a semigroup. For finite Markov chains we identify a canonical lumping obstruction and quantify its failure. Conditional expectations give orthogonal martingale packets, and the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup gives a countable Hermite model. Bayesian updating is treated as normalized transfer. We characterize exact coarse sufficiency, determine the coarsest nontrivial fixed sufficient partition for a likelihood family when the common level sets are nontrivial, and split relative information into coarse and local terms. Positive fractional powers are handled through spectral, Balakrishnan, and subordination formulas. Green operators, finite differences, and finite state Feynman--Kac formulas provide analytic realizations. Schur--Feshbach elimination produces a rational self-energy and an exact memory kernel. Every stable finite hidden system yields a polynomial exponential expansion, including Jordan blocks. A certified optimal primary block selection and a Volterra estimate control reduced trajectories. State dependent killing, survival laws, moments, and competing risks complete the finite theory.

One parameter semigroups provide a common language for evolution equations, Markov processes, diffusion, and resolvent methods. Standard analytic foundations appear in \cite{Pazy1983,EngelNagel2000}. Finite Markov chains and their coarse descriptions are treated in \cite{KemenySnell1960,Norris1997,RogersPitman1981}. Conditional expectation and martingale difference decompositions are basic parts of probability theory \cite{Williams1991}. Gaussian transfer and Hermite expansions provide a spectral model for the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup \cite{Janson1997}. Fractional powers of generators and subordinate semigroups belong to the functional calculus of positive and sectorial operators \cite{Balakrishnan1960,SchillingSongVondracek2012}. The Feynman--Kac formula, projection methods, and phase type laws add three further views of transfer \cite{Kac1949,Feshbach1958,Zwanzig1961,Neuts1981}.

The final sections move from generators to source reconstruction and hidden variables. The one-dimensional Dirichlet Green kernel is reproduced exactly by the scaled inverse of the second difference matrix at grid nodes. A discrete maximum principle gives a complete second order error estimate for smooth Poisson solutions. Finite state Feynman--Kac transfer is proved in discrete and continuous time. Schur--Feshbach elimination yields the exact projected resolvent, the retained memory equation, and the Laplace correspondence between memory and self-energy. Every stable finite hidden system gives a polynomial exponential memory expansion. Primary blocks can be ranked optimally for the certified \(L^1\) bound, and a Volterra estimate carries kernel error to the retained solution. Survival, event density, moments, and competing risks are then read directly from a transient semigroup.

In probability, the same structure appears in several forms. Markov transfer is linear and exact lumpability is the vanishing of a canonical kernel obstruction. Conditional expectation is an orthogonal stochastic projector whose differences form martingale packets. The Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup resolves exactly into Hermite packets. Bayesian transfer is nonlinear because of evidence normalization. Its exact two stage decomposition separates coarse packet evidence from local conditional change. Relative entropy then records exactly how much information lies at each level. A fixed sufficient coarse description exists for every prior precisely when the likelihood is constant inside each packet. The common level sets of a likelihood family give its unique coarsest fixed sufficient partition.

Positive fractional powers preserve exact intertwining. Under a common spectral gap, the Balakrishnan formula turns an ordinary generator defect into an explicit fractional defect. Green operators and finite differences show how source reconstruction fits the same transfer language. Feynman--Kac weights Markov paths by a potential without leaving the semigroup framework.

Hidden packets provide the final structural lesson. Exact elimination does not erase them. It returns them as a rational self-energy in the resolvent and a causal memory kernel in time. The primary decomposition of the hidden generator produces every finite memory kernel as a finite sum of polynomial exponential modes. Stable blocks can be truncated with an integrated error certificate, and the Volterra estimate transfers that certificate to the retained trajectory. State dependent killing identifies the Feynman--Kac potential with a survival mechanism. Survival and competing risks are then scalar reconstructions of a transient semigroup.
